newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia proposes major changes to mining rules.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia proposes major changes to mining rules.

text.p: Indonesia has proposed sweeping changes to its mining regulations that industry sources said on Thursday give the government more control in the aftermath of the Busang scandal but could subdue the investment climate.
The proposals came in the form of amendments to the seventh-generation contracts of work (COW), which were approved in principle last year and accepted by mining companies.
M. Simatupang, vice-chairman of the Indonesian Mining Association (IMA), said foreign companies had been given until next Tuesday to indicate if they wanted to negotiate.
"Foreign mining companies which had applied for the COW were very concerned over the proposed changes, especially because the COW had been given approval in principle," he told Reuters.

"The companies are in a crisis. The companies were initially told to take it or leave it, but the director-general of mining has since told the IMA, it's up to the companies to negotiate...to accept or whatever," he said.
In a related development, a senior mining official on Thursday briefed coal mining companies on a new contract of work for the industry.
Industry sources said the contract was aimed at bringing the coal sector in line with mineral mining, and that the briefing was held by the director of coal mining, Soedjokotirto Soekotjo.

"Mr Soedjoko gave a briefing this morning to coal mining companies about the contract of work," an official at the department of coal mining told Reuters. Industry officials said the contract had yet to be approved by parliament.
The proposed changes to mineral mining contracts include:

* When carrying out a feasibility study, the mining company shall give the government a 10 percent share in the company on a free carried interest basis, or a bigger share depending on the economic viability of the project.

* If the company discovers additional mineral reserves during the operational period and/or increases its annual production above the level approved by the government in the feasibility study, the government's share in the company will be increased proportionately.
* The company shall offer some of its shares to co-operatives or to a company owned by a regional government.

* When shareholders of the company or its holding company obtain capital gains as a consequence of publishing information owned by the company on a stock exchange outside Indonesia, then the capital gains would be allocated to the shareholders of the company in proportion to their equity.

* If the company wishes to obtain additional capital by making a public offering, the offering must be done on the Indonesian stock exchange. A public offering of the company, however, may be made outside Indonesia.
* All data should not be made public without consent of the government. Such data should be evaluated by a third party consultant which has been appointed by the company with government approval.
* The company's reserves calculation/estimation must be done by an independent consultant appointed by the government, with the cost being borne by the company.
* By the sixth year of operations, all posts other than that of directors must be filled by Indonesian nationals.
* The company must consult the government on the allocation of the company's budget for regional development planning.
"The proposals are hard to follow," one senior foreign mining executive said. "They are not practical or desirable."

"The whole advantage of the COW system is fixing the rules of the game for the future. Mining is a very capital intensive, long-term business, not like a shoe factory where there's a relatively fast payout of the capital investment," he said.

He said the proposals could dent the investment climate and smacked of rising nationalism after the Busang incident, when local companies and the government clamoured for stakes in what turned out to be the biggest mining swindle in history.

Canadian mining company Bre-X Minerals Ltd declared that Busang contained 71 million ounces of gold, making it the biggest find this century, but an independent audit found the property nearly worthless and the data falsified.
State Secretary Murdiono said on Thursday the government would be consistent with its mining rules that allow 100-percent foreign owned companies to operate in the sector.
"The government must be consistent. The government will uphold the law," he told reporters.
"Who said it is compulsory," he said when asked about the 10-percent stake to be given to the government. "If it is an idea it's okay, but we must implement the rules."
Investment Minister Sanyoto Sastrowardoyo said: "It is a new thing. I don't know what the reasons are or the motivation."
